property_summary: For every bytes4 interfaceId input, the correct contract returns true from supportsInterface(interfaceId) exactly when interfaceId equals IAccessControl or IERC165 interface id (i.e., it recognizes IERC165 and IAccessControl), while the mutant fails by not recognizing IERC165 (so there exists an interfaceId — namely type(IERC165).interfaceId — for which the mutant returns a different boolean than the reference).

For every bytes4 interfaceId input, the reference contract C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId or interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (i.e. it recognizes IERC165 and IAccessControl); the mutant breaks this by returning false for type(IERC165).interfaceId, so there exists an interfaceId (fuzzable) for which the mutant's return differs from the reference.

For every bytes4 interfaceId input, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId equals type(IERC165).interfaceId (it recognizes IERC165) but the mutant returns false for that id, so there exists an interfaceId (fuzzable) where mutant's return differs from the reference.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId or interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant incorrectly returns false for type(IERC165).interfaceId, so there exists an interfaceId (fuzzable) where the mutant's return differs from the reference.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference C.supportsInterface returns true when interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId (it recognizes IERC165); the mutant returns false for that interfaceId, so there exists an interfaceId (fuzzable) where the mutant's return differs from the reference.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true for IERC165's interfaceId (0x01ffc9a7) and also returns true for IAccessControl's interfaceId when queried (i.e. supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) == true); the mutant that always returns false breaks this by returning false for those ids.

For every 4-byte interface id, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true for IERC165's interface id (0x01ffc9a7) and for IAccessControl's interface id when applicable, whereas the mutant that always returns false will return false for at least those interface ids (so the general rule is: supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) must be true for all inputs; the mutant violates this).

For every 4-byte interfaceId the reference C reports that it supports the ERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) when queried (i.e. supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) returns true); the mutant that always returns false will return false for that interface id, violating this rule for that input.

For every 4-byte interface id, the reference contract always returns true when queried for the ERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId); the mutant that unconditionally returns false will return false for that id, so the property is: calling supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) MUST succeed and return true for all inputs — the mutant breaks this by returning false for that specific interface id.

For every bytes4 id, calling supportsInterface(id) on the reference contract completes and returns true when id equals the IERC165 interface id (0x01ffc9a7) while the mutant that always returns false will return false for that same id; thus the reference must report support for IERC165's id and the mutant breaks that.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true iff the interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. only supported interface IDs), while the mutant incorrectly returns true for all interfaceIds; the property checks that supportsInterface(falseRandom) is false for at least some fuzzed id and that reference never returns true for an unsupported id.

For every interfaceId, the reference contract returns true for IERC165 or IAccessControl interface ids only (i.e., there exist some ids for which supportsInterface returns false), whereas the mutant returns true for all ids, so there exists an interfaceId for which reference supportsInterface(...) == false but mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true iff the id equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. some interfaceIds are unsupported), whereas the mutant always returns true; thus there exist interfaceIds for which the reference returns false but the mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface either returns true only for genuinely supported interfaces (as implemented via ERC165/IAccessControl logic) or false otherwise; the mutant always returns true for every interfaceId, so there exist interfaceIds where the reference returns false but the mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) never returns true for the zero interfaceId (0xffffffff is also conventionally unsupported) unless it equals IERC165 or IAccessControl; the mutant returning true unconditionally will make supportsInterface(0x00000000) (or another specific fuzzed id) return true while reference returns false — so pick a fuzzed id and assert that when C.supportsInterface(id) is true then id equals one of the known supported ids (IERC165 or IAccessControl); the mutant will violate this for some fuzzed id.

For every role and account, the reference contract's hasRole(...) returns true exactly when the account is recorded as a member of that role (i.e., hasRole(role,account) == _roles[role].members[account]); the mutant inverts this boolean and therefore will return the opposite for some inputs.

For any role and account, the reference contract's hasRole(role, account) returns true exactly when that account was granted the role via _setupRole (i.e., hasRole equals the stored membership); the mutant inverts this result and thus for some role/account pairs the return value differs (true vs false).
For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) returns the stored membership boolean; the mutant inverts that result, so there exist role/account pairs where hasRole differs (true vs false).

For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) returns the stored membership boolean (true iff the account is a member); the mutant inverts that boolean, so for some fuzzed role/account pairs the returned value differs.

For every role and account, hasRole(role, account) returns whether that account is recorded as a member of the role in storage (so hasRole(role,account) == true if the account was set up as a member and == false otherwise); the mutant inverts this boolean so there exist role/account inputs where the return value differs.

For every (role, account) pair, the reference contract returns hasRole(role, account) == (whether that account was granted the role via _setupRole in constructor or other calls); the mutant always returns false, so there exist inputs (role, account) where reference returns true but mutant returns false.

For any (role, account) input, the reference contract's hasRole returns true for accounts that were granted that role in the constructor (e.g. address(this) or the deployer) while the mutant always returns false; thus there exist fuzzed (role, account) pairs for which reference.hasRole(role,account)==true but mutant.hasRole(role,account)==false.

For every (role, account) input, calling hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract never returns false for accounts that were granted that role in the constructor (notably address(this)); the mutant always returns false, so there exist inputs where the reference returns true but the mutant returns false.

For every (role, account) input, if the contract constructor granted account a role then hasRole(role, account) always returns true on the reference; the mutant that always returns false will violate this for some role/account granted in the constructor.

For every role/account pair, calling hasRole(role, account) on the reference returns true for accounts that were granted the role (e.g. address(this) or address(c)) while the mutant always returns false; thus there exist fuzzed (role,account) inputs where reference.hasRole(...) == true but the mutant returns false — we assert that at least one of the constructor-granted roles is observed true by the reference for the fuzzed role/account inputs (the mutant will fail for those).

For every role and account, the real contract's hasRole(role, account) returns the stored membership (i.e., can be false for arbitrary inputs), whereas the mutant always returns true — so there exist inputs (role, account) where hasRole is false in the reference but true in the mutant.

For every role/account pair, the reference contract's hasRole(...) returns the stored membership (so querying a freshly unused role/account may be false); the mutant always returns true, so there exist fuzzed role/account inputs where reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For any role/account, the reference contract's hasRole either returns true only for accounts explicitly granted that role (so there exists at least one role/account pair where hasRole is false); the mutant always returns true, so there exist fuzzed role/account inputs where the reference returns false but the mutant returns true.

For any role and account, calling hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract never always returns true for arbitrary fresh role/account pairs unless that account was explicitly granted the role via the contract's public interface; the mutant breaks this by returning true for all inputs (including pairs that are not granted).
